subject: Automotive & EVs
title: Understanding Five-Star Ratings
description: A quick win: understand Understanding Five-Star Ratings.

hook.text: A five-star crash rating sounds perfect, but what it actually measures may surprise you.

buildup.text: Each star covers a specific test—frontal impact, side impact, and rollover resistance.

discovery.text: Five stars means the driver faces less than a 10 percent chance of serious injury in that crash.

twist.text: Two five-star cars can differ hugely—one may ace frontal tests but barely pass side impacts.

climax.text: Smart buyers read each individual test score, not just the headline star number.

punchline.text: Five stars doesn't mean equally safe in every crash.

quiz.question: What does a five-star frontal crash rating roughly indicate?
options: Less than 10% serious injury risk in that test

details.summary: Five-star safety ratings translate complex crash test data into a simple consumer-friendly scale, letting buyers quickly compare how well different vehicles protect occupants in various collision scenarios.
details.whyItMatters: Star ratings create powerful market incentives. Manufacturers compete fiercely for five stars because consumers use these ratings to make purchasing decisions, driving continuous safety improvement.
takeaways: Stars summarize performance across multiple crash test types
Different agencies like NHTSA and Euro NCAP use their own scales
Ratings evolve over time as testing standards become stricter

faq.question: Are five-star ratings consistent across different countries?
faq.answer: No. NHTSA, Euro NCAP, and other agencies use different tests and criteria. A five-star car in one system may not receive five stars in another, so ratings are not directly comparable across programs.

faq.question: Has the meaning of five stars changed over the years?
faq.answer: Yes. Testing criteria become stricter over time. A five-star car from 2005 would likely score lower under today's standards because new crash scenarios and active safety requirements have been added.
